sense.text: This is David’s psalm. “Thou hast possessed my reins”: the Lord possessed his mind. “Thou hast covered me in my mother’s womb”: David is speaking of how he was covered, while he was being made, in his mother’s womb.

“I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” He is wonderfully made because the Lord formed him before he was ever formed in the womb, in his book, like an art book. Everything about him was already written.

“My substance was not hid from thee”: his substance is his body. “When I was made in secret” means in the womb, and “the lowest parts of the earth” is the womb of the woman, where he was “curiously wrought.”

“Thine eyes did see my substance”: the Lord already saw David’s body before he was even put in the womb, because he wrote it down. It is all written. “Yet being unperfect” means not fully made yet, still in development.

“In thy book all my members were written”: God has a book. When he creates us there is a book open before him, a blueprint of what he wants put in and what he wants left out: your hair, your eyes, your skin, your height. All your body parts are written. The Lord has everything about you written down.

“Which in continuance were fashioned”: first it was unperfect, not fully formed, and then in continuance it was fashioned. “When as yet there was none of them” is the embryo, the early stages of development in the womb. David is letting us know that before any of that even takes place, everything is written down: how that child will be formed, how he or she will look, the hair, the colour, the eyes. That is what the Lord is saying here.

precepts.why:
Solomon says “thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit, nor how the bones do grow in the womb of her that is with child.” Men call it the miracle of childbirth, the mystery of childbirth. They do not know how a child’s body is formed, how the bones are formed in the womb. We don’t understand that.

“Even so thou knowest not the works of God who maketh all.” What David was made in secret, in the lowest parts of the earth, is the work of God, and no man can explain it.

This is the mother who had seven sons and watched them all tortured for the honour of the Lord. She gives this speech as she is witnessing it, before she herself underwent the same thing: “I cannot tell how ye came into my womb: for I neither gave you breath nor life, neither was it I that formed the members of every one of you.”

So the Lord is behind the forming of the body in the womb, the members written in his book. He is behind it, truly in detail.

“But doubtless the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man, and found out the beginning of all things, will also of his own mercy give you breath and life again, as ye now regard not your own selves for his laws’ sake.” Even though you are going to die today, you will return again. She believed it. We understood back then the resurrection of the dead; it was not foreign to us. And she also pointed out that she did not know how they were formed in her womb, because the Lord is the one behind it.

sense.text: Nicodemus, “a ruler of the Jews”, came to Christ by night. And Christ answered him: “Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” The conversation at hand here is being born again. This whole class revolves around being born again, being born of fire and water. What does that mean?

“How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?” Nicodemus said, what are you talking about, being born again? You are going to climb back into your mother’s womb when you are already grown? Nicodemus had no idea what Christ was talking about.

“Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.” Being born again means being born of water and of the Spirit.

When the class came back to this verse, after the water had been opened up, it came plain: the water is wisdom, God’s laws, and the Spirit is the same. Both the water and the Spirit go back to God’s laws, God’s commandments, and the faith of his Son. That is what Christ is talking about.
“That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.” There is a distinction between the two.

“The wind bloweth where it listeth.” The wind is the word of God. When we go out and bring forth the word of God to our people, we don’t know who is listening, who is being affected by it, who’s listening and who’s not. The Lord doesn’t let us know that, because if we understood where the wind blows it would get to our heads. We would become egotistical, get ahead of ourselves and become arrogant. So the Lord doesn’t allow us to see how large this movement is.

Some Israel say the Israelite movement is a joke and isn’t taken seriously. France says something very different: they outlawed our congregation out there, and if people are caught listening to us they can be fined. If a whole damn government is passing laws on us teaching, someone is taking it seriously. We march through Oakland, California, watched by hundreds and thousands in the street with helicopters flying over us, and there is no news footage. When we marched in the Bronx, a brother who was a reporter and photographer took picture after picture in awe, trying to write an article, and his publisher, an Israeli so-called, said no, don’t put that out there, because they run and control the media. We are blackballed, we are blacklisted. This movement is taken very seriously.

“And thou hearest the sound thereof”: you hear the sound because we are in the street teaching. You hear the mic, the brothers reading aloud with power. Cry loud, spare not. You hear the wind. “But canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit”: those that hear the word.

precepts.why:
What is the spirit? A lot of Christians think it is just a puff of smoke that goes inside of you while you do nothing: keep no commandments, keep no laws, just believe and you are full of the spirit. Yeah, of Satan. Of God? No.

“There is one that accuseth you, even Moses, in whom ye trust.” A lot of Israelites read the law, read the Bible, and the law accuses them all the time. They commit acts against the laws of God and don’t see it.

“For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.” Moses wrote of Christ all throughout Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy; you find Christ all through the law. “But if ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words?” So the words that Christ spoke were the words of Moses, and the prophets also spoke the words of Moses.

“It is the spirit that quickeneth”: quickeneth means gives life. “The flesh profiteth nothing.” Remember what Christ said to Nicodemus: that which is born of the Spirit is spirit, that which is born of the flesh is flesh. The flesh is sin, and it profits nothing.

“The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.” The words Christ spoke unto us are the words of Moses and the prophets. So the words of the Bible, the Bible itself, is the word of life: the words of Moses and the prophets and the apostles and Christ himself are the words of life. That is the spirit you must be born of.

We are still dealing with what the spirit is. “Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.”

“For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin.” So the laws of God are spiritual. The laws of God going back to Moses and the prophets, and the apostles and Christ himself, are spiritual. They are the spirit that Christ spoke of: the words that are spirit and life.

“For the thoughts of mortal men are miserable, and our devices are but uncertain.” Mortal men, covered in this flesh, have miserable thoughts, because we always have worries, concerns, trauma, issues, drama, malfunctions, dysfunctions. Our devices are our plans, and they are uncertain. Man plans, God laughs: we can have a plan and God says, no, you’re not doing that, that’s a stupid idea, because our fleshy mind gives us stupid thoughts sometimes.

“For the corruptible body presseth down the soul.” The corruptible body is this flesh that covers us. That’s why Christ said the spirit quickeneth and the flesh profiteth nothing. “And the earthy tabernacle weigheth down the mind that museth upon many things”: the flesh grows old by the day. Once you’re born, that’s the countdown to your death. You can work out and try to extend it, but it ages regardless; you can’t fight against time. That’s why our forefathers made it clear the best thing to celebrate is death: you get that new body that never dies, doesn’t wither, doesn’t age, and doesn’t weigh you down with miserable thoughts. Paul called this body vile. Our fathers didn’t celebrate birthdays; there was no point when you are born in captivity. That’s why babies cry when they’re born: they know where they’re at. The mind that museth upon many things is a mind all over the place in captivity: bills, car notes, rent, mortgage, kids, clothes.

“And hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth”: we have an idea, but we don’t know everything, because we are mortal fleshly men and women. What we do understand, we understand through labour, research, trying to figure it out. “But the things that are in heaven who hath searched out?” The things in heaven go back to this Bible: who has searched out the things in this Bible? “And thy counsel who hath known, except thou give wisdom, and send thy Holy Spirit from above?” To have counsel of what is wisdom, God must send his Holy Spirit from above to you, to understand what was required of you in heaven.

“For so the ways of them which lived on the earth were reformed.” Reformed: remember David said how he was formed in the belly, and Christ told Nicodemus, be born again. It all goes back to when you are born. Reform comes from the Latin, to form again, to shape again: re, again, and form, to form. Reformed is being born again, formed again, remade.

And you can learn a lot from babies, because that is exactly what we become when we repent. When you repent and come into this truth you literally become a newborn all over again. You have to crawl. Your eyes are weak; you can barely see what’s going on, because you’ve been in darkness. Where is the child? In the womb, in darkness. Where were you before you came to the truth? Darkness. It is the exact same thing. When you read the Bible at first you don’t see things clearly, until you develop and grow; then you start to see like a baby sees, and the first thing you do is start drinking the milk.

How are you reformed? “Men were taught the things that are pleasing unto thee, and were saved through wisdom.” You are reformed because you are taught the things that please your God, the things searched out in heaven, and saved through wisdom, which is God’s commandments. There are layers behind what Christ said to Nicodemus.

sense.text: “Cause Jerusalem to know her abominations.” “Thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother an Hittite.” The Lord is calling us Hamites. He’s insulting us, name calling, because of our abominations in verse 2, the things we were doing. You act just like the Hamites I had you go and kill out of the land; that’s your father and mother there.

“And as for thy nativity”: as for your birth. “In the day thou wast born”: he is talking about when we were in Egypt in captivity. Is he talking about an actual birth? No. When a child is born the navel has to be cut, so he is speaking spiritually. “Thy navel was not cut” means you were still attached to your mama.

“Neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all.” You weren’t washed off, you weren’t rinsed in salt water, and you weren’t even wrapped in a blanket. Salt is like a cleanser; you weren’t salted, and you weren’t swaddled.

“None eye pitied thee, to do any of these unto thee”: no one cared about you, to do these things for you as a baby. “Thou wast cast out in the open field, to the lothing of thy person”: you were hated.

“In the day that thou wast born”: we became a nation in the land of Egypt. That is when we were born; that is when our nation formed, our nativity.

“When thou wast in thy blood, Live.” That goes back to being quickened, in John 3. It was time for us to live, because when we were in Egypt we were dead, in darkness: unclean, unwashed, not swaddled, navel not cut, not salted, hated and loathed.

“I have caused thee to multiply as the bud of the field”: going back to Egypt. “Thy breasts are fashioned, and thine hair is grown, whereas thou wast naked and bare.” Look at you now, all grown up: hair on your head, clothes on. You got fat, put on weight like a baby, got plump.

“I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee.” That’s how you know it’s Egypt. We got older; our nation grew bigger and bigger. Then the Lord had compassion on us and sent Moses to go and get us. He wrapped us, took care of us, nurtured us. “And thou becamest mine”: we became his when he took us out of Egypt. That is when he made a covenant with us. He is giving us the time frame.

“Then washed I thee with water; yea, I throughly washed away thy blood from thee, and I anointed thee with oil.” God gave us his laws and his commandments; that is how he washed us. He was trying to reform us, because we were born in Egypt with that slave mind: navel not cut, covered in blood, unswaddled. The Lord said, I let you grow, I took you out of there, I washed you up, I told you how to live, I anointed you with oil and gave you water. You got all fat and nourished up, and what did you go and do? Disrespect me. I raised you up, and look what you do.

precepts.why:
Solomon makes what Ezekiel said a little simpler. “For the whole creature in his proper kind was fashioned again anew.” The whole creature is Israel, the whole family of Israel, his creation, the whole nation. It was fashioned, as David said in Psalm 139 about being formed, and fashioned again anew: made again, born again.

How? “Serving the peculiar commandments that were given unto them, that thy children might be kept without hurt.” That is how he washed us with water and anointed us with oil; that is what the Lord was talking about through Ezekiel. So to be born again you must be keeping the peculiar commandments. That is how you are fashioned again anew: the navel, the umbilical cord, is cut, you are rinsed in salted water, you are swaddled, you are nursed, and you grow. That is God’s nourishment, God’s nurturing. The seed, the culture God gave us, the commandments: that is what nourishes the baby to be born.

“When Israel was a child, then I loved him”: this goes right back to Ezekiel 16, Israel as a baby. “And called my son out of Egypt.”

That is twofold. It goes into Christ being called out of Egypt, where his parents fled with him, and it goes into Israel itself, when we were taken out of Egypt and the Lord cut our navel, washed the blood off of us, salted us, anointed us with oil, washed us with water and put us in swaddling clothes. It alludes to Christ first and foremost, and to the nation itself: we were “fashioned again anew,” born again, “serving the peculiar commandments.”

Solomon is speaking, and he says exactly what David said: “I myself also am a mortal man, like to all, and the offspring of him that was first made of the earth.” The one first made of the earth is Adam.

“And in my mother’s womb was fashioned”: fashioned, the same word David used, “to be flesh in the time of ten months, being compacted in blood, of the seed of man.” The child is of the seed of man. Man produces life; the woman births life. We produce, they bring forth. We beget, they birth. “And the pleasure that came with sleep”: sleeping in the womb.

“And when I was born, I drew in the common air”: he breathed his first breath, “and fell upon the earth,” came out of the womb, as we all do. “And the first voice which I uttered was crying, as all others do”: here we go again, I’m back.

“I was nursed in swaddling clothes, and that with cares.” Remember Ezekiel said we weren’t swaddled at all; here he says I was nursed in swaddling clothes. When a child is first born you wrap them up real tight in the blanket, and with cares, because children are very fragile; their bones are very soft. This is prophecy: he is speaking of himself, but he is going into someone else.

“And she brought forth her firstborn son”: that’s Christ, “and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.” It was Passover; the inn was crowded. Wrapped in swaddling clothes, what an interesting coincidence: that is what Solomon said.

“And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.” That was the sign: a babe in a manger wrapped in swaddling clothes, just like Solomon. The son called out of Egypt is the one who was swaddled, where Israel in Egypt was not swaddled at all.

sense.text: “For thou art alone, and we all one workmanship of thine hands.” We are one workmanship of his hands.

“For when the body is fashioned now in the mother’s womb”: keep hearing that word, fashioned, over and over again. “In the mother’s womb”, as we read earlier in Psalms and in Ecclesiastes 11:5. “And thou givest it members”: the members which are written in his book.

“Thy creature is preserved in fire and water.” Keep that word preserved in mind. How is a baby preserved in fire and water? Physically speaking, the fire is the heat in her womb, and the water is what the child is surrounded by, the fluid, the sack. That is science. But there are layers to this.

“And nine months doth thy workmanship endure thy creature which is created in her.” There is a reason behind why the Lord allows a child to form within that time frame. What does a child undergo as they grow in the womb? Change.

We go through fire and water in the womb, and we go through fire and water outside of it too, and we grow thereby the same way outside the womb as we do in the womb. That is how a man is born again.

precepts.why:
First the fire. “Behold, I will make my words in thy mouth fire.” The words of God, this Bible, are the words of fire. The word of God is fire because it burns the hearts and minds and spirits of the wicked when they hear it.

But fire is not only something used to harm. It is also used to heal, to cleanse and to fix; fire is a cleansing agent. So the words of God can be the fire that refines us and makes us better, or we rebel against them and get destroyed by the fire that is yet to come. Fire goes both ways.

“Is not my word like as a fire? saith the Lord; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” The word of God is strong when it is against the wicked.

Often when we sit in class and hear the word of God, if you have a conscience, if God is dealing with you, you feel conflicted: a certain level of guilt or shame. It burns, it hits your soul a certain way. Some people cry; some people go home and reflect and examine themselves, because the word of God is hard, and depending on how it is brought out it can hit hard. But if the person is wicked and rebellious, it burns and they get mad, bitter and angry, and they leave, or they walk around with bitterness in their heart and don’t last long. They get broken in pieces: their spirit gets angry, they get offended, and they’re gone. The word of God is fire both ways.

“He that feareth the Lord will do good, and he that hath the knowledge of the law shall obtain her.” The context is the knowledge of the law.

“He himself made man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his counsel”: he made Adam and left Adam in his counsel; he gave Adam his laws. “If thou wilt, to keep the commandments, and to perform acceptable faithfulness.” Faith is a performance, not a thought or a feeling. Faith is a performance, an act: works, doings. The apologists have the audacity to use the Septuagint against us; Sirach is in the Septuagint, and if they read this it would destroy them.

“He hath set fire and water before thee.” But you already had that set before you in the womb: you are preserved in fire and water. Then you come out of the womb and fire and water are set before you again. Why? So you can develop like the child in the womb, so you can grow and be born again.

“Stretch forth thy hand unto whether thou wilt”: you make the choice. “Before man is life and death; and whether him liketh shall be given him.” Whichever you choose, you are going to get. But you are going to go through both, fire and water, and you are going to receive your reward.

sense.text: “The sea is set in a wide place, that it might be deep and great.” The sea is water: a deep ocean.

“But put the case the entrance were narrow, and like a river”: there is an entrance, a path, to this deep ocean, but it is very narrow. The river leads to the ocean. “If he went not through the narrow, how could he come into the broad?” You have to go through the narrow first; the narrow leads to the wide.

“A city is builded, and set upon a broad field, and is full of all good things: the entrance thereof is narrow, and is set in a dangerous place to fall”: it is set on a cliff. “Like as if there were a fire on the right hand, and on the left a deep water.” There it is again, fire and water, leading to that city that is builded, leading to the kingdom.

From the time you are in the womb you face fire and water. When you are in the world and you repent and come out of the world, you are faced with fire and water all over again, all the way until the time of your death. You are between the fire and the water.

“And one only path between them both, even between the fire and the water, so small that there could but one man go there at once.” Every man works out his own soul salvation with fear and trembling. You can’t save your kids, you can’t save your wife, you can’t save your husband. You go one at a time.

“If he never shall pass the danger set before it, how shall he receive this inheritance?” He can’t. He has to walk through the fire and water, the path between the two. Remember: life and death, fire and water, set before you. And what are you preserved in, in the womb? Fire and water.

“Even so also is Israel’s portion. Because for their sakes I made the world”: he made the world for Israel. “And when Adam transgressed my statutes”: Adam messed up, “then was decreed that now is done,” the narrow path leading to the city that is builded.

“Then were the entrances of this world made narrow.” When Adam was there the entrance was wide; he got right in. But because of him the path was made narrow, enough for one person to walk at a time. “Full of sorrow and travail”: that is the fire and the water. “Full of perils”: danger. “And very painful”: going through that fire and that water you are either in danger of being burned or in danger of being drowned. It is a narrow path: strict, straight, severe, dangerous.

“For the entrances of the elder world were wide and sure, and brought immortal fruit.” The beginning world, with Adam and Eve, was wide and sure to get in. There was no death, no danger, no perils, no evil, no problems, nothing.

“If then they that live labour not to enter these strait and vain things, they can never receive those that are laid up for them.” You have to labour; you have to work for it. That is why the fire and water were set there in the first place. The strait things are that straight and narrow path between the fire and the water, and whoever will not labour can’t get into that city.

“Nevertheless the righteous shall suffer strait things”: the righteous will walk through that path and suffer perils, dangers, travail, sorrow, pain, the things between the fire and the water. Because you are preserved in that fire and that water, you must endure both, as a child does in the womb. “And hope for wide”: to get to that city at the end of the path.

“For they that have done wickedly have suffered the strait things, and yet shall not see the wide.” The wicked are going to suffer things too, but they are going to die. They are not getting the kingdom at all; they are going to die and die again.

“There is no judge above God, and none that hath understanding above the Highest.” Ezra was trying to ask things above his pay grade, to go beyond and understand the Lord. The Lord said, you are a mortal man; you can’t begin to comprehend what I’m talking about.
“Because they despise the law of God that is set before them.” Remember in Sirach 15, what was set before you is fire and water, life and death: the commandments of God. Those are the strait things.

“For God hath given strait commandment.” The commandments of God are very straight, very strict. You can’t go to the one side or you fall in the fire; you can’t go to the other side or you drown. The commandments of God are very clear; there is no way around it. Christians say you don’t have to keep it, because they don’t want the path. They want to just die, and they get their wish.

“What they should do to live, even as they came, and what they should observe to avoid punishment”: to avoid the pain after death.

precepts.why:
“Enter ye in at the strait gate.” This is the same path Ezra was shown; that is where Christ got it from. The same strait gate, the same straight path between the fire and the water.

“For wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction.” If you are not facing any difficulties, trials or tribulations while keeping these laws and commandments, you are going through that wide gate, and you ain’t making it. This truth is not easy. It is going to be hard, and it is going to get harder as time goes on. Watch the news: the white man is starting to revert to what he was in the 60s, 50s, 40s, back through the 1800s and 1700s. The smile he had on his face when he saw a Negro is starting to fade. And black folks are not prepared for it, because when they see him they see God. He can sit there and speak his hate to their face, and they say, he’s just angry, he’s going through things, come let me hug you. That’s the apologist.

The man who passed away, that white folks are losing their minds over, talked crazy about black folks: he spoke evil about Martin Luther King and said black people are violent, and black folks are crying over him, saying we lost a good one. You are the ones going through the wide gate. And the Lord had it where he suffered the very violence he spoke of. God is a very ironic God; he does things to remind you, don’t talk about his people too much.

“Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.” Why few? Because black folks do not want the hard; they want the easy, instant gratification. The other nations deal with longevity: they do things knowing it will affect us 100, 200, 300, 400 years down the line; they have plan A, and if A fails they have B and C set already. Black folks have no plan at all: do or die. They don’t want difficulty, accountability, reality, responsibility. Men will teach that the men of the Bible were free and had rulership, but won’t teach how to go about it: be warmed and filled. When it comes to ignorance, chaos and stupidity, black people and brown people find safe haven among themselves. White folks labelled their own and said, that’s not all of us; black folks call ill behaviour culture and heritage, a black thing. No, it is a slave thing, a slave-minded thing.

Few find that straight path, because it is easier to do nothing and expect God to do everything: keep no laws, no commandments, do whatever I want and just believe, and I’m good. That is the wide gate.

“My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation.” That goes back to the straight path, the fire and the water, the perils, dangers, sorrows and travails. “Set thy heart aright”: set your mind right, “and constantly endure” that straight path, the trouble, Jacob’s trouble that is coming. “And make not haste in time of trouble”: don’t get weak, don’t run. This truth is blood in, blood out; there is no running from it. Christ died for you; we owe him. There is nowhere to go.

“Cleave unto him, and depart not away, that thou mayest be increased at thy last end. Whatsoever is brought upon thee take cheerfully, and be patient when thou art changed to a low estate.”

“For gold is tried in the fire.” Fire is twofold: a cleaning instrument and a destructive instrument. It does both. “And acceptable men in the furnace of adversity.” Adversity goes back to the strait things, troubling times. You will lose your family, your friends, your children. Some will lose their jobs, their homes, those closest to them, and many of us are going to lose our lives here when things get real bad. The church is the people, not the building, and many of us are going to be faced with a choice. That is why acceptable men are tried in the furnace of adversity.

The Lord referred to Egypt as the iron furnace, and that is where we are now: America is a spiritual Egypt, and it is the iron furnace too. You are either going to go through this fire and come out better, or you are going to burn along with it.

“But the Lord hath taken you, and brought you forth out of the iron furnace, even out of Egypt.” He called literal Egypt the iron furnace: hot misery, affliction, persecution. We went through all of that in Egypt, and likewise we will do so in Egypt again, here.

Egypt is called the iron furnace because acceptable men are going to go through that fire, “to be unto him a people of inheritance.”

“For they be thy people, and thine inheritance, which thou broughtest forth out of Egypt, from the midst of the furnace of iron.” We are back in the iron furnace, and they are heating it.

A furnace takes a while to get hot. In the civil rights era the furnace was cooling down some: black folks got jobs, joined unions, used the white man’s toilet, sat at the front of the bus, and thought we made it. No: the furnace is getting hot now. White folks are being real honest now. They call it climate change, global warming; that is exactly what it is, and only black folks are still in it. They call it ICE; they should call it fire. The northern kingdom is getting dragged in the street, and they damn sure don’t feel no ice. You feeling it now? The iron furnace.

“But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and there shall no torment touch them.” Deacon Isaac said it best: when they leave this world, they mourn for us, because they are in paradise. Their leaving is sad for us, not for them; they are in a better place, and we are in the worst place to be. No torment touches them; the torment awaits us.

“In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die”: in the sight of the wicked, the heathen, even our people, they seem to be killed, murdered off. “And their departure is taken for misery,” because there will be torture going on, “and their going from us to be utter destruction: but they are in peace.” They are at rest. “For though they be punished in the sight of men, yet is their hope full of immortality”: back to that builded city.

“And having been a little chastised, they shall be greatly rewarded.” God calls torture and death a little chastisement. A little. “For God proved them, and found them worthy for himself. As gold in the furnace hath he tried them,” and the iron furnace is here, “and received them as a burnt offering,” because they got killed.

“Two parts therein shall be cut off and die; but the third shall be left therein.” Many of us are going to die, especially here in America; a lot of us are going to be destroyed entirely.

“And I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried.” Tried in the iron furnace: the iron furnace called captivity, and the iron furnace called a body. This fleshly body is a damn furnace too. “They shall call on my name, and I will hear them: I will say, It is my people: and they shall say, The Lord is my God.”

“And I will turn my hand upon thee, and purely purge away thy dross, and take away all thy tin.” What is he talking about? The dross and the tin are all the impurities, and he takes all that away.

“Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil.” That goes back to being reformed, being refined in the fire, so that the acceptable come through.

“Then shall they be known, who are my chosen; and they shall be tried as the gold in the fire.” Then it will be known who are the chosen, who are worthy: those tried as gold in the fire, as the psalmist said.

The baby is preserved in the fire and in the water; the path set before us is fire and water; and the chosen are tried by fire. That is the fire. Next comes the water.

sense.text:
Now the water. “That he might sanctify”: keep that word in mind, “and cleanse it.” It is the church, and the church is Israel, the Israelites.

“With the washing of water by the word.” The word of God is the washing of water. The word of God is the water that sanctifies and cleanses us, that removes the tin and the dross out of us, that refines us.

The fire is refining or destructive, and the water is also refining or destructive. If there is a deep sea you can drown; the waves hit you and you’re done. Water is a cleansing agent, but it is also a destructive element, as fire is.

precepts.why: “Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.” The clean water is the word of God. Is he talking about Deer Park, bottled water from the store? No. He is talking about God’s commandments, his laws. That is the water.

“The word of God most high is the fountain of wisdom; and her ways are everlasting commandments.” The fountain is water: the word of the Most High is the fountain, and its ways are the everlasting commandments.

Write this one down next to Ephesians 5:26. “With the bread of understanding shall she feed him, and give him the water of wisdom to drink.” Wisdom feeds him, and gives him the water of wisdom to drink.

So the water is wisdom: God’s laws. It goes back to verse 1 of the same chapter: “he that hath the knowledge of the law shall obtain her.”

Read again now: “Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.” Now we have an idea what the water is, and what the Spirit is.

Both go back to God’s laws, God’s commandments, and the faith of his Son. That is what Christ was telling Nicodemus: the water and the Spirit you must be born of are the word that washes, “the washing of water by the word.”

sense.text:
Back to Ezra, so as not to lose the thought. “For when the body is fashioned now in the mother’s womb”: and refashioned again, when you repent. “And thou givest it members”: it grows. “Thy creature is preserved in fire and water.”

“And nine months doth thy workmanship endure thy creature which is created in her.” Nine months the mother endures the child growing within her. The child is growing within the mother, undergoing growth, and with growth comes change. Now, preserved: still going back to being born again.

precepts.why:
“And by a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt.” By a prophet, Moses, the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt: going back to Ezekiel 16:1-9.

“And by a prophet was he preserved.” Remember through Ezekiel the Lord said our navel was not cut, we were not washed, and we were not salted. What does salt do? Salt preserves; it is a preservative. The commandments of God are referred to as salt.

Who was preserved? The nation of Israel was preserved by Moses. When Moses gave us the commandments of God, he gave us that salt in ourselves. We became fashioned again anew, serving the peculiar commandments, as Wisdom of Solomon 19:6 says.

“Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour”: if we stop keeping the commandments of God, “wherewith shall it be salted?” What is it worth? “It is thenceforth good for nothing.”

Because what is salt good for? Preserving. Preservation, preserves, preservatives: it is all the same. That is what the commandments do for us: they keep us from hurt.

“Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves.” What is the salt? The commandments of God, that preserve you and keep you alive. If you have salt in you, you are preserved. “And have peace one with another”: be at peace with one another.

“Neither do men put new wine into old bottles.” The new wine goes into the commandments of God: that is the new man. When you are fashioned again anew, when you become a new creature, you have to put old things away, because the new can’t be kept in the old; otherwise it is no good. New wine in old bottles will not hold; the bottle is worn out, and it rips.

“Else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish.” If the body is not changed, it is not going to hold the commandments; it will not keep the commandments of God. If you are still in the world doing worldly things while keeping the commandments of God, you can’t serve both. Eventually it leaks out: after a while you are going to be offended, and you’re going to fall out. If you are going to be new, you have to be new all the way through.

“But they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.” That is being born again: new wine in a new bottle. You keep the commandments of God, you are able to preserve the commandments, and you preserve yourself.

“Remember Lot’s wife.” Why does it start with that? Lot’s wife looked back because she loved the world she was in, rather than escaping that flame. She looked back, she got destroyed, and she was turned to salt.

“Whosoever shall seek to save his life shall lose it.” If you seek to save or preserve your life in this world, you are going to be destroyed: seeking to save your worldly lifestyle, your job, your worldly family, kids, mothers, fathers, holding on to worldly things. That is the new wine in the old bottle: it ain’t going to hold for long. Eventually it runs out of you, because you haven’t fully changed; the wine is new, but the body and the mind are the same.

“And whosoever shall lose his life shall preserve it.” Whoever loses his life, whoever dies, is killed for this truth, shall preserve his life: not this life here, the life to come. You are going to come back again, better, and live forever. It is the same as the little chastisement in Wisdom of Solomon 3: the torment, and then peace.

“Let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee.” The prisoner is us. The sighing of the prisoner is our prayers in the time of affliction, persecution, temptation, trouble, perils and dangers.

“According to the greatness of thy power preserve thou those that are appointed to die.” That is why Christ said, those that seek to save their life lose it, and those that lose their life preserve it. They are at peace. The mother with the seven sons: they’re good; they are sealed.

“And render unto our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom their reproach, wherewith they have reproached thee, O Lord. So we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever.” The Most High is making it clear our neighbours, the nations, are going to face a fierce reproach and judgment, sevenfold into their bosom, for what they did against us. But we get preserved. We are going to be all right.

This whole psalm is about preservation: preserve, preserve, preserve. “The Lord shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.”

“The Lord shall preserve thy going out”: leaving this world, “and thy coming in”: coming into this world, “from this time forth, and even for evermore.” Those who are predestined to be preserved are going to be preserved regardless. Whether they die or live, going out or coming in, they are preserved. They’re good.

“It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel.” The preserved of Israel are the elect of us.

“I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles”: the Gentiles here are the northern kingdom, not the other nations; they get the light during their slavery. “That thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth”: because Israel is scattered throughout all the ends of the earth, and that is where salvation is going to be brought to them.

sense.text: “Thy creature is preserved in fire and water”: preserved in fire, and preserved in water. Now the fire and the water come back together.

precepts.why:
“And Eleazar the priest said unto the men of war which went to the battle.” Notice Eleazar is speaking to the men of war. “Only the gold, and the silver, the brass, the iron, the tin, and the lead”: these are the metals.

“Every thing that may abide the fire, ye shall make it go through the fire, and it shall be clean.” Fire is a cleansing agent as well as a destructive one. “Nevertheless it shall be purified with the water of separation.” Then it goes to the water. So it is cleaned through fire and purified through water, because water is a destructive agent as well as a cleansing agent. The water of separation is the water of sanctification: separation sanctifies; it is made holy.

“And all that abideth not the fire ye shall make go through the water.” What can’t go through the fire goes through the water. But it is supposed to go through both.

Eleazar spoke to the men of war about the gold and the silver. Who is Paul talking to? “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.” Endure hardness: that goes into the fire, the affliction, the sorrow, the travail, the narrow, the strait things. A good soldier is a man of war.

“No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.” Now you know who he is talking to: the same men of war that Eleazar spoke to, the ones who must pass through the fire and the water.

sense.text:
“But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour.” The great house is Israel. The same thing as in Numbers 31.

The vessels of honour are the gold and the silver. In the Old Testament it is the gold, the silver, the brass, the tin, the lead: those are the vessels of honour, because they can deal with the fire and the water. Some can only deal with the water: the wood and the earth, the vessels of dishonour.

“If a man therefore purge himself from these”: purge himself from the wood and the earth, because they can’t deal with the fire. The wood and the earth are of no value when you have to deal with both the fire and the water. You must be preserved in both; the water is not enough.

“He shall be a vessel unto honour”: the gold and the silver, the metal, which can endure the fire and the water. “Sanctified”: separated, like the water of separation, going back to Ephesians 5:26, where he sanctifies with the washing of water by the word. “And meet for the master’s use”: useful in the Lord’s army. “And prepared unto every good work.” So we must all put ourselves in the mind to prepare ourselves as vessels useful for honour: sanctified vessels of honour.
“Flee also youthful lusts”: youthful lust goes back to the vessels of dishonour. “But follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace”: faith, charity and peace are the gold and the silver.

precepts.why: “That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour.” The vessel is the body: this vessel. In sanctification and honour, a vessel of honour. Now we have insight into what Paul means by vessels and honour in Timothy: the body that is purged and sanctified.

Why is Paul speaking of vessels of honour, of gold and silver as opposed to wood and earth that can’t survive the fire? Where is he getting that from? “How is the gold become dim! how is the most fine gold changed! the stones of the sanctuary are poured out in the top of every street.”

He explains who the most fine gold is: “The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter!” We went from gold to earth. We cannot endure the fire; we became vessels of dishonour. “The daughter of my people is become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness.” The sons of Zion have become dim and earthen, and the women have become wicked and hateful. Both of us underwent a terrible, degenerate transformation. Now as a nation we are earthen vessels as opposed to golden ones.

“They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets”: in our kingdom we ate good things, healthy things, lawful things, dressed well and were honoured well; now we are in the streets. “They that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills.” Brought up in scarlet and silk and beautiful fabrics, now we are in the ghetto and the slums. We call it the trap, and we call it the culture. Yeah, I’m from the hood: we embrace it. Pissy elevators, bums everywhere, crackheads on the corner: that is the dunghill. We used to have scarlet, silk, gold and silver; now we have Temu and Shein, Ross, JCPenney, Walmart and Kmart, because we are in captivity. Don’t be offended; we wear it too. Two watches for $10, them big astronaut sneakers: to us that is fine gold now. That ain’t scarlet, that ain’t silk, that ain’t gold and silver.

“For the punishment of the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the punishment of the sin of Sodom, that was overthrown as in a moment, and no hands stayed on her.” In Sodom they died; they got burned and were gone. We are suffering it generation after generation. Hands remain on us to this very day: we are getting hung from trees and they call it suicide, organs are being trafficked, sex trafficking is going on. Sodom was destroyed and gone, melted away in the fire; we are here suffering, and we embraced the dunghill. Our punishment is far worse than Sodom’s.

Why does Paul use the term vessels of honour? “Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood. For when Moses had spoken every precept to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of calves and of goats, with water, and scarlet wool, and hyssop.” The blood of calves and goats represented Christ’s own blood, with water.

“And sprinkled both the book, and all the people.” Why the people? “Saying, This is the blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you. Moreover he sprinkled with blood both the tabernacle, and all the vessels of the ministry.” He sprinkled the book, he sprinkled the temple, and he sprinkled the vessels of the ministry, and that is us too.

We are the vessels of this ministry. Aside from the blood of Christ being upon us, it goes deeper: we are the vessels of his great house that the blood of Christ was sprinkled upon. That is why it was sprinkled on the book and on us, because we are supposed to be those vessels of honour that were in the temple. They represent us. Paul’s great house represents that temple, and we are that great house.

“And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth.” We might be sanctified, made vessels of honour, through the truth. What is the truth? The Psalms say it: the law is the truth, and all his commandments are truth.

Christ says it plainly: “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” What were Christ’s words? The laws and the commandments. So we are sanctified through his laws, his commandments.

“Thy righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and thy law is the truth.” And: “Thou art near, O Lord; and all thy commandments are truth.” So the commandments of God are the truth that Christ said we are sanctified through. We are sanctified through his laws, his commandments, and that sanctifying is what makes a vessel unto honour.

John says: “I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire.” The fire in this context is not the good one.

“Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner.” We are that floor that needs purging, and the wheat is us too. “But he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.” He will burn up the undesirable, those that seek the broad, the wide; they are not making it in. There will be nothing of them left. That is cleaning too: cleaning house, getting rid of all the wicked. It is still cleaning, regardless.

“And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly.” Wholly means fully, completely: new wine and a new bottle, both completely new and changed. Born again.

“And I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” In keeping the commandments you are preserved: your spirit, your soul and your body. Whether you are alive, or dead and gone, you will be resurrected, get the kingdom, and be preserved blameless until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Back to that great house with the vessels of honour and dishonour. “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble.” Wood, hay and stubble are the vessels of dishonour; gold, silver and precious stones are the vessels of honour.

“Every man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it.” What day? The days to come: the dangers, trials, tribulations and temptations that will manifest who is the gold, the silver and the precious stones, and who is the wood, the hay and the stubble that cannot endure the fire as well as the water. “Because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is.” It will reveal who is honourable in this truth and who is dishonourable. You have to go through the fire. You can learn the commandments all you want; if you don’t go through the trials and tribulations of the fire, you ain’t making it. Then you are that wood, that stubble, that earth, that hay: the chaff.

“If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward”: he built on gold, silver and precious stones that fire cannot destroy. “If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss”: those in the congregation, in the body, who are wood, hay and stubble are going to fall out. But the honourable will maintain the building of the house until it is time for us to go home. “But he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.”

“Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?” We are those vessels of honour; we represent the temple Solomon built and the tabernacle Moses built. That is why Moses sprinkled the blood on us: we represent that body, that temple, that great house. The Spirit of God dwells in you as it did in the temple. “If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy”: he will not make it through the water and the fire. “For the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are.”
